sections.title: Gender, Power and the Archive
sections.description:
Feminist writers use the term reproductive justice to describe bodily autonomy, especially the right to have children, the right to not have children, and the right to parent children in safe and sustained communities. This first-year seminar examines popular writing in newspapers, magazines, books, posters, reports, and manifestos that reflect the history of reproductive justice. Students will read a wide range of twentieth- and twenty-first-century texts that analyze the role of gender, power, and reproduction. We will look at popular representations of pregnancy and motherhood, queer parenting, and other forms of kinship. Our class will be held in Penn’s Kislak Center for Special Collections, and each week we will work with archival and primary source materials that reflect this history and allow us to analyze the evolution of reproductive justice in the context of their original print culture.
Through our engagement with archival sources, this seminar will also introduce debates in archival studies, with special attention paid to how archival silences, unrecorded histories, and institutional gaps can be understood not simply as absences but as active sites for theoretical reflection. Rather than positioning feminism against the archive, we will explore how archival methods and feminist theory mutually enrich one another and help us access new knowledge and perspectives on gender and power. Students will be asked to read assigned texts carefully, and assignments will include in-class participation, short presentations, and several short writing assignments on their independent research with archival sources.
